## Appendix A Numerical Techniques

We rely on Chebyshev interpolation to numerically solve the zero mode equations of motion (3.4). This method is one of several numerical approaches used for collocation: the discretization of partial differential equations (PDEs) to transform them into matrix equations. Here we give a brief introduction; more details can be found in [74, 75].

Chebyshev interpolation provides a method of approximating a smooth function $f(\zeta)$ on the interval $\zeta\in[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ using its values at a finite and discrete set of points. That is, given the function $f(\zeta)$ evaluated at the set of Cheybshev points,

$$ \zeta_{k}=\cos\left(\frac{\pi(2k+1)}{2(N+1)}\right)\,,\mathrlap{\qquad k=0,\ldots,N}\,, $$

we may approximate it at any point in $\zeta\in[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ via the interpolant

$$ f_{N}(\zeta)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}f(\zeta_{k})p_{k}(\zeta) $$

where the functions $p_{k}(\zeta)$ , defined such that $p_{k}(\zeta_{n})=\delta_{kn}$ , are the degree- $N$ Lagrange polynomials associated to the points (A.1). Importantly, the Lagrange polynomials can be reliably evaluated away from the interpolation points using the second barycentric form [76, 75],

$$ p_{k}(\zeta)=\frac{w_{k}}{\zeta-\zeta_{k}}\,\Bigg/\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{w_{n}}{\zeta-\zeta_{n}}\,, $$

where we introduce the Chebyshev weights

$$ w_{k}=\sin\left(\frac{2\pi k(N+2)+\pi}{2(N+1)}\right)\,,\mathrlap{\qquad k=0,\ldots,N\,.} $$

The interpolant (A.2) then provides a degree- $N$ polynomial approximation that exactly agrees with $f(\zeta)$ at the points $\zeta_{k}$ and has an error which decays exponentially in $N$ for all other points on the interval.

The interpolant (A.2) allows us to represent the function $f(\zeta)$ as a $(N+1)$ -component vector $\vec{f}=\{f(\zeta_{k})\}$ . We can similarly represent derivatives of this function working with the derivative matrices $p^{\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})$ and $p^{\prime\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})$ , defined by [75, 77]

$$ \displaystyle p^{\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n}) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{w_{k}/w_{n}}{\zeta_{n}-\zeta_{k}}&n\neq k\\
-\sum_{k\neq n}p^{\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})&n=k\end{cases}\,\,\,, \displaystyle p^{\prime\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n}) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}2p^{\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})p^{\prime}_{n}(\zeta_{n})-\frac{2p^{\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})}{\zeta_{n}-\zeta_{k}}&n\neq k\\
-\sum_{k\neq n}p^{\prime\prime}_{k}(\zeta_{n})&n=k\end{cases}\,\,\,. $$

Any differential equation for $f(\zeta)$ on the interval $\zeta\in[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ can then be approximated by a matrix equation for the function values $\{f(\zeta_{k})\}$ by substituting (A.2) for $f(\zeta)$ , evaluating the equation at each Chebshev point $\zeta_{k}$ , and using (A.5) to convert differentiation into matrix multiplication. This matrix equation can then be solved by any number of standard numerical techniques.

For example, the equation

$$ \left[\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\zeta^{2}}+g(\zeta)\right]\!f(\zeta)=0\,, $$

for any regular function $g(\zeta)$ on $\zeta\in[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ can be approximated by the matrix equation

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{N}\left(\mathcal{D}_{2}+\mathcal{G}\right)_{nk}f(\zeta_{k})=0\,, $$

where $(\mathcal{G})_{nk}=g(\zeta_{k})\delta_{nk}$ , $(\mathcal{D}_{2})_{nk}=p_{k}^{\prime\prime}(\zeta_{n})$ , which is defined in (A.5), and the number of nodes is chosen to be $N+1$ . The solutions to (A.6) are then well-approximated by the interpolant (A.2) constructed from the null space of the matrix $(\mathcal{D}_{2}+\mathcal{G})$ . As long as $N$ is large enough, this interpolant then provides an approximate solution to (A.6) whose pointwise error decays exponentially in $N$ .

When the equation we aim to solve is defined on the semi-infinite line $r\in[0,\infty)$ , we must first map it to the interval $\zeta\in[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ to apply Chebyshev interpolation. We find that the simplest map, the linear fractional transformation

$$ \zeta(r)=\frac{r-L}{r+L}, $$

works well, where $L$ is a tuneable parameter that broadly controls which $r$ values are sampled by the corresponding Chebyshev nodes (A.1). In practice, we take $L$ to be an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ number times the scale over which the solution varies naturally (set by $\mu^{{\scalebox{0.5}[0.85]{$-$}}1}$ for the equations we are interested in) though we ensure that our solutions do not depend on the precise choice of $L$ .

For two-dimensional equations of motion like (3.4), we have a choice in how to apply Chebyshev interpolation. The simplest approach is to expand in Fourier modes, as in §3.1, to reduce the problem to a system of coupled ordinary differential equations. That is, we expand each spinor component into their lowest $2J+1$ Fourier modes

$$ \psi_{\alpha}(r,\varphi)=\sum_{|\ell|\leq J}\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(r)\,{{\mathrm{e}}}^{i\ell\varphi}\,, $$

such that (3.4) reduces to a finite set of coupled equations (3.6) involving $2\times(2J+1)$ mode functions. We can then interpolate each radial function $\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(r)$ with $N+1$ nodes to convert (3.6) into a $2\times(2J+1)\times(N+1)$ -dimensional linear equation. The profiles displayed in Figure 2 were generated with $J=41$ and $N=61$ , though our results are robust to changing both $J$ and $N$ .

Another approach is to interpolate the spinor components $\psi_{\alpha}(x,y)$ using a two-dimensional Cartesian grid. This requires first mapping both $x$ and $y$ from $({\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}\infty,\infty)$ to $[{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{$-$}}1,1]$ . We do so via two different maps

$$ \zeta(x_{i})=\begin{cases}\arctan\hskip 0.5pt({x_{i}}/{L_{i}})&0\leq m/\mu\leq 0.8\\
\tanh\hskip 0.5pt({x_{i}}/{L_{i}})&0.4\leq m/\mu\leq 0.95\end{cases}\,, $$

depending on the value of $m/\mu$ , where $x_{i}=\{x,y\}$ . Here, the parameters $L_{i}=\{L_{x},L_{y}\}$ determine the relevant scales in the original $x$ or $y$ coordinate. These maps efficiently sample small $(x,y)$ values while avoiding numerical artifacts at large $x$ and $y$ . Since the solutions elongate in the $x$ -direction as $m\to\mu$ , we used $L_{x}\simeq\mathcal{O}(1)\times 1/(\mu-m)$ and $L_{y}\simeq\mathcal{O}(1)\times\mu^{{\scalebox{0.5}[0.85]{$-$}}1}$ . We find that with these ranges of $L_{x}$ and $L_{y}$ , our Cartesian results agree with each other for overlapping $m/\mu$ and that our solutions are independent of our specific choice. For large numbers of nodes, $N_{x},N_{y}\geq 90$ , our results obtained with a Cartesian grid agree with those obtained using a Fourier mode expansion, but formulating the problem in the Fourier basis is significantly faster.

Finally, to compute the moments of our solutions and properly normalize them, we must numerically evaluate integrals involving these profiles. We do so via quadrature, in which the integral is approximated by a weighted sum of the function’s values on the Chebyshev grid. Explicitly, an arbitrary integral of the density $|\psi(r,\varphi)|^{2}=|\psi_{0}(r,\varphi)|^{2}+|\psi_{3}(r,\varphi)|^{2}$ can be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}r\,a(r,\varphi)\hskip 0.5pt\hskip 0.5pt|\psi(r,\varphi)|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha,n,\ell,\ell^{\prime}}{}\int_{{\scalebox{0.5}[0.85]{$-$}}1}^{1}\!\mathrm{d}\zeta\,\int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\mathrm{d}\varphi\,r^{\prime}(\zeta)a_{n}(\zeta)\hskip 0.5pt{{\mathrm{e}}}^{in\varphi}{{\mathrm{e}}}^{i(\ell-\ell^{\prime})\varphi}\hskip 0.5pt\psi^{\phantom{*}}_{\alpha,\ell}(\zeta)\hskip 0.5pt\psi^{*}_{\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}(\zeta) \displaystyle=2\pi\!\sum_{\alpha,k,\ell,n}q_{k}\hskip 0.5pt\hskip 0.5ptr^{\prime}(\zeta_{k})\hskip 0.5pta_{n}(\zeta_{k})\hskip 0.5pt\psi^{\phantom{*}}_{\alpha,\ell}(\zeta_{k})\hskip 0.5pt\psi^{*}_{\alpha,\ell+n}(\zeta_{k})\, $$

where

$$ q_{k}=\int_{{\scalebox{0.5}[0.85]{$-$}}1}^{1}\!\mathrm{d}\zeta\,p_{k}(\zeta) $$

is the quadrature weight, which can be efficiently numerically evaluated, and

$$ a(r,\varphi)=\sum_{|n|\leq J,k}a_{n}(\zeta_{k})p_{k}(\zeta){{\mathrm{e}}}^{in\varphi} $$

is an arbitrary weight function, whose $n$ ’th Fourier mode has value $a_{n}(\zeta_{k})$ at $r(\zeta_{k})$ . For instance, to normalize the profile functions in Figure 2, we evaluate (A.11) with $a(r,\varphi)=1$ , while to compute the dipole (5.11) we choose $a(r,\varphi)\propto r\cos\varphi$ and $a(r,\varphi)\propto r\sin\varphi$ .

## Appendix B Multipole Moments

In this Appendix we provide more details on the derivation of the worldsheet effective action given in (5.8). We follow the method in [72], adapted to the case of a string. Our starting point is the term in the action that couples the gauge field to the four-dimensional current from (5.6), which is pointing along the axion string,

$$ S_{\textsc{em}}=-\!\int\!\mathrm{d}^{4}x\;j^{\mu}A_{\mu}. $$

As in the main text, we take $\mu=0,1,2,3$ , $a=0,3$ , and $i,j,k_{i}=1,2$ .

Our goal is an effective action describing these interactions which is valid when the wavelength of the gauge field is much larger than the characteristic size of the source. In this regime, we can Taylor expand the gauge field about the string source at the origin,

$$ A_{\mu}(t,\vec{x})=-\!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\;x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\big[\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n}}A_{\mu}\big]_{x=(t,0,0,z)}. $$

Since our source of interest points along the string (see 5.6), we can drop the terms with $\mu=1,2$ . We are left with the action

$$ S_{\textsc{em}}=-\!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\!\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\,\frac{1}{n!}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}j^{a}\!\hskip 0.5pt(t,\vec{x})\big[\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n}}A_{a}\big]\!\hskip 0.5pt(t,z). $$

It is useful to rewrite the action in terms of gauge invariant quantities. We first consider the $A^{0}$ term, and note that $E^{k_{i}}=F^{0k_{i}}=\dot{A}^{k_{i}}+\partial_{k_{i}}A^{0}$ . This allows us to exchange radial derivatives of $A^{0}$ for time-derivatives of $A^{k_{i}}$ and terms involving the electric field, $E$ . We find,

$$ \begin{split}S_{A_{0}}=&-\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}r\;j^{0}\big[A^{0}\big]\!\hskip 0.5pt(t,z)-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{0}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\big[\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}E^{k_{n}}\big]\!\hskip 0.5pt(t,z)\\
&+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}r\;j^{0}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\big[\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}\dot{A}^{k_{n}}\big]\!\hskip 0.5pt(t,z)\end{split} $$

The last term in this expression can be combined with the $A^{3}$ term of (B.3) to get a gauge invariant term involving the magnetic field. To see this, we integrate by parts within the ${\rm d}^{2}\sigma$ integral, and use current conservation: $\partial_{0}j^{0}=-\partial_{3}j^{3}$ . This allows us to rewrite,

$$ \begin{split}\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{0}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}\dot{A}^{k_{n}}&=\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;(\partial_{3}j^{3})\;x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}A^{k_{n}}\\
&=-\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}\partial_{3}A^{k_{n}},\end{split} $$

where in the last equality we have integrated by parts again. With this replacement, the sum of the last term of (B.4) and the $A^{3}$ term from (B.3) is

$$ \begin{split}S_{B}=&-\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}A_{3}-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}\big(\partial_{3}A^{k_{n}}\big)\\
&-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial{k_{n-1}}\big(\partial_{k_{n}}A_{3}\big)\\
=&-\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}A_{3}-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\partial_{k_{1}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n-1}}\epsilon^{3k_{n}j}B_{j},\end{split} $$

where we have used $\partial_{i}A_{3}-\partial_{3}A_{i}=F^{i3}=\epsilon^{3ij}B_{j}$ . Adding back the remaining terms in $S_{A^{0}}$ and relabeling indices, we obtain the full action

$$ \begin{split}S_{\textsc{em}}=&-\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;(j^{0}A_{0}+j^{3}A_{3})-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}rj^{0}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{2}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n}}E^{k_{1}}\\
&-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;j^{3}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{2}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n}}\epsilon^{3k_{1}j}B_{j},\end{split} $$

which can be written in terms of the field strength as

$$ \begin{split}S_{\textsc{em}}=&-\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\int\!{\rm d}^{2}r\;(j^{0}A_{0}+j^{3}A_{3})-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\!\mathrm{d}^{2}\sigma\left[\int\!{\rm d}^{2}rj^{a}x^{k_{1}}\!\cdots x^{k_{n}}\right]\partial_{k_{2}}\!\cdots\partial_{k_{n}}F_{k_{1}a}.\end{split} $$

This action reduces to (5.8) using the current (5.6) and the normalization condition for $|\mathcal{F}(r,\varphi)|^{2}$ .
